practice_questions.text:
Which type of malware encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the decryption key?
A) Spyware
B) Ransomware
C) Worm
D) Key-logger
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B) Ransomware.

practice_questions.text: State two types of malware that could be used to attack a business's computer system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two from: virus / worm / Trojan horse / spyware / ransomware / key-logging software. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by social engineering and why it poses a risk to an organisation's data.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a correct definition of social engineering (manipulating people rather than systems). 1 mark for an example such as phishing. 1 mark for explaining the risk, e.g. employees may unknowingly hand over credentials or install malware.

practice_questions.text: Describe, with an example, how a DDoS attack could affect an online retail business.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining what a DDoS attack is (flooding a server with traffic). 1 mark for explaining the immediate effect (server overwhelmed, website goes down). 1 mark for a specific business impact (customers cannot place orders / loss of sales). 1 mark for a further consequence such as loss of customer trust or reputational damage.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the financial and legal implications of a data breach for a medium-sized business that holds customer personal data.
practice_questions.marks: For financial implications: direct costs such as ransom payment, forensic investigation, customer compensation, IT security upgrades (up to 3 marks). For legal implications: fines under UK GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018, mandatory reporting obligations, possible prosecution (up to 3 marks). Credit linkage between the two, e.g. legal fines compound financial loss. Full marks require both dimensions to be discussed with developed reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the threats posed by hacking and malware to a school that stores student records digitally. Consider the impact on the school, students and any legal obligations. In your answer, weigh up which threat is likely to cause the greatest harm.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8 marks): Balanced evaluation comparing hacking and malware, justifies which poses greater harm with reasoned argument, demonstrates understanding of both technical and human factors, references UK GDPR / DPA 2018, sustained quality of written communication throughout. Secure (5–6 marks): Clear explanation of multiple threats, impacts on school and students (financial, reputational, loss of service, data manipulation), reference to relevant legislation. Developing (3–4 marks): Some explanation of hacking and/or malware impacts with reference to the school context. Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic identification of threats with limited explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an input device?
A) Monitor
B) Printer
C) Microphone
D) Speaker
practice_questions.marks: C) Microphone [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between a hard disk drive (HDD) and a solid state drive (SSD).
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two correct contrasting points: HDD uses spinning magnetic platters / SSD uses flash memory chips with no moving parts; HDD is slower to access data / SSD is faster; HDD is more fragile (moving parts) / SSD is more durable; HDD is cheaper per gigabyte / SSD costs more per gigabyte. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of RAM in a computer system.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. “RAM stores data temporarily”). Development to 2 marks: “RAM holds programs and data that are currently in use by the CPU, allowing fast access without reading from a slower drive.” Full 3 marks: add that RAM is volatile — its contents are lost when power is removed — so programs and files must be saved to secondary storage to be kept permanently. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A school is setting up a new reception desk. Identify two suitable input devices and explain why each is appropriate for that environment.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per device identified + one mark per explanation. Example: Barcode reader — the receptionist can scan visitor badges or library books quickly without typing, reducing errors (2 marks). Touchscreen — a touchscreen sign-in system is intuitive for visitors with no prior training and does not require a separate keyboard or mouse (2 marks). Accept any suitable device with a valid, contextualised justification. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A small business currently stores all its files on a single internal hard disk drive. The owner is considering switching to solid state drives and adding cloud storage.

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of making this change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Balanced discussion covering SSD advantages (faster boot and file access, no moving parts so more durable, quieter) and disadvantages (higher cost per gigabyte, limited write cycles over time). Cloud advantages (accessible from any location, automatic off-site backup, scales easily) and disadvantages (requires an internet connection, ongoing subscription cost, data held by a third party raises privacy questions). Interaction noted: the two technologies complement each other — SSD for fast local access, cloud for backup and remote access.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two points on each side with some development.
Developing (2 marks): Points largely one-sided or undeveloped.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A video editor works from a home studio and needs to transfer large 4K video files between their workstation and a client’s laptop.

Evaluate which storage and port options would best meet their needs, justifying your recommendation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Identifies that 4K files are very large (tens of gigabytes), so speed and capacity are the primary criteria. Recommends an external SSD over a USB flash drive (faster read/write, more durable, higher capacity available) and USB-C or USB 3.0 port (high transfer speeds). Considers the client’s laptop may not have USB-C, so an adaptor or USB-A fallback should be available. Evaluates cloud alternatives — convenient but upload/download of multi-gigabyte files requires fast broadband and time. Reaches a justified conclusion: external SSD via USB-C is the most practical combination for large, time-sensitive file transfers.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two relevant recommendations with justification and some comparison.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but limited comparison or justification.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with little application to the scenario. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes "information" in an ICT context?
A) Raw facts and figures entered into a computer system
B) Data that has been processed by a computer to give it context and meaning
C) Rules applied to data to reach a conclusion
D) A file stored on a hard drive
practice_questions.marks: B) Data that has been processed by a computer to give it context and meaning [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using ICT to store data compared with a paper-based system.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct advantages from: fast search and retrieval / automated backups / simultaneous multi-user access / easy sorting and reporting / large storage capacity / data can be processed to produce reports. Answers that repeat the same idea score 1 mark only. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by encoding data and give one benefit of doing so.
practice_questions.marks: Encoding definition (up to 2 marks): converting data into a shorter or standardised representation, e.g. using M/F instead of Male/Female or 1/0 for Yes/No (2 marks for a clear definition with example; 1 mark for a basic definition without example). Benefit (1 mark): any one from — reduces storage space / speeds up searching and sorting / reduces input errors by limiting choices. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between lossless and lossy compression and give one example file type for each.
practice_questions.marks:
Lossless (2 marks): compression that reduces file size without permanently removing any data — the file is identical to the original when decompressed; example: PNG or ZIP (1 mark each, max 2 for lossless).
Lossy (2 marks): compression that permanently removes some data to achieve a greater reduction in file size — the file cannot be perfectly restored; example: JPEG or MP3 (1 mark each, max 2 for lossy). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: A school stores student records in a database. Give two characteristics of good-quality data and, for each, explain why that characteristic matters for this school database.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for naming a valid characteristic plus one mark for a relevant explanation, repeated for a second characteristic. For example: accuracy (1) — if a student's medical information is recorded incorrectly, the school may give the wrong first aid response in an emergency (1); up to date / currency (1) — if a home address is outdated, the school cannot contact parents in an emergency (1). Other valid characteristics: completeness, relevance. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A small business is deciding whether to move from paper-based records to a digital ICT system for storing customer data.

Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using ICT to store data for this business, and recommend whether the move is worthwhile.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation covering multiple advantages (fast retrieval, large capacity, multi-user simultaneous access, automated backup, easy production of reports) and disadvantages (security risks including hacking and malware, ongoing costs for hardware/software/security, hardware failure risk, legal compliance obligations under data protection law, staff training needed). A substantiated recommendation is given — e.g. the move is worthwhile for a growing business because the efficiency gains outweigh the risks, provided security measures are implemented and staff are trained, but a very small business with few records and limited IT expertise might find the costs and risks disproportionate.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two advantages and two disadvantages, some developed, a recommendation attempted.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points largely one-sided or undeveloped.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic relevant points with no development or recommendation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of system software?
A) Microsoft Word
B) Google Chrome
C) Microsoft Windows
D) Adobe Photoshop
practice_questions.marks: C) Microsoft Windows [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between open-source software and proprietary software.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two correct contrasting points: open-source source code is publicly available / proprietary source code is kept private; open-source is usually free / proprietary usually requires a licence fee; open-source can be legally modified by users / proprietary cannot; open-source may have community support / proprietary usually has dedicated commercial support. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the purpose of utility software and give one specific example.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition (software that maintains the computer). 2 marks for development (e.g. utility software runs maintenance and optimisation tasks in the background to keep the system running efficiently and securely). 3 marks for adding a specific, accurate example with a brief explanation of what it does (e.g. anti-malware software scans the system for malicious programs and removes them to protect user data). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A hospital uses a database management system to store patient records and appointment data. Identify the software category this belongs to and explain two advantages it offers the hospital over storing records on paper.
practice_questions.marks: Category: information-handling software [1 mark]. One mark per advantage up to 2 marks, one mark per explanation up to 2 marks: e.g. records can be searched instantly using a query, whereas paper records must be searched manually (2 marks); multiple authorised staff can access the same record simultaneously from different terminals, which is not possible with a single paper file (2 marks). Accept any valid, contextualised advantage. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A freelance graphic designer is considering switching from proprietary design software to an open-source alternative.

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of making this change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Advantages — eliminates licence fees (relevant for a freelancer with limited income); source code is available so the software can be customised for specific workflows; supported by a community of developers who contribute updates. Disadvantages — may lack features available in the industry-standard proprietary tool; clients and collaborators may use different file formats, causing compatibility issues; technical support may be limited to forums rather than a dedicated helpdesk; staff training would be needed to switch tools. A balanced conclusion noting that the decision depends on the designer's client base and required features.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two points on each side with some development.
Developing (2 marks): Mostly one-sided.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A large retail company is reviewing the software used across its 50 stores. Currently, staff use a general-purpose spreadsheet to process sales, track stock and communicate with head office.

Evaluate whether replacing the spreadsheet with specialist point-of-sale software and a dedicated communication platform would be beneficial for the company.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Identifies problems with the current setup — a spreadsheet was not built for real-time stock tracking across 50 sites or for processing transactions quickly at a checkout; errors are likely and data must be manually updated. Specialist POS software advantages: designed for retail transactions, integrates with stock databases automatically, produces sales reports, reduces errors and speeds up service. Communication platform advantages: structured message threads, file sharing, video calls and persistent records replace ad-hoc emails and improve coordination between stores and head office. Counter-argument: implementation costs, staff retraining across 50 sites, risk of downtime during switchover, and potential data migration difficulties. Substantiated conclusion: for a business of this scale, specialist software is likely to deliver long-term efficiency gains that justify the upfront investment, but a phased rollout is recommended to minimise disruption.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two benefits per software type with some comparison and an attempt at a conclusion.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but limited comparison or application.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with little development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of logical protection?
A) Keeping a server in a locked room
B) Employing security guards to patrol the building
C) Using encryption to scramble stored data
D) Storing backup drives off-site
practice_questions.marks: C) Using encryption to scramble stored data [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two physical protection methods an organisation can use to keep its data safe.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct methods from: locks / biometrics / location of hardware / backup systems / security staff. Answers must clearly identify a physical method; vague answers such as "keeping data safe" score 0. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a firewall helps to protect an organisation's network from unauthorised access.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. "a firewall blocks unwanted traffic"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "a firewall examines data packets entering and leaving the network, comparing them against a set of rules, and blocks any traffic that does not meet those rules"). A further developed explanation or reference to hardware vs software firewalls scores 3 marks (e.g. add "this prevents hackers from establishing unauthorised connections to internal systems, even if the organisation's own devices have been compromised"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what an acceptable use policy is and give one example of a rule it might contain.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): an acceptable use policy (AUP) is a documented agreement between an organisation and its staff that sets out what employees are and are not permitted to do when using the organisation's ICT systems (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement that it is a set of rules for computer use).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, the AUP might state that staff must not install personal software on work computers, because unauthorised software could contain malware that compromises the whole network (2 marks for a specific, applied example with a reason; 1 mark for a vague example without explanation). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A small business stores customer payment details on a local server. Last month it suffered a ransomware attack that encrypted all its files and demanded a ransom. The business had no backup copies of its data and no disaster recovery plan.

Discuss the protection measures the business should put in place to prevent a similar incident and to recover more effectively in future.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two categories of protection with developed explanation and clear reference to the scenario. For example: anti-malware software would detect and block ransomware before it executes; encryption protects confidentiality if data is stolen, but does not stop ransomware encrypting files; a regular off-site backup strategy ensures that if files are encrypted by ransomware, a clean copy can be restored without paying the ransom; a disaster recovery plan ensures staff know exactly what steps to take, minimising downtime. Discussion notes that multiple layers are needed because no single measure is sufficient.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two measures identified and explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two measures identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A large hospital stores patient medical records digitally. It employs a team of IT security staff, uses biometric scanners on all server room doors, requires multi-factor authentication for all staff logins and enforces a strict acceptable use policy.

Evaluate the extent to which the hospital's current security measures are sufficient to protect patient data from all types of threat.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation acknowledging the strengths of the existing measures — biometrics prevent unauthorised physical entry to server rooms; multi-factor authentication makes remote account compromise very difficult; the AUP reduces risk of human error; security staff provide active monitoring. Counter-argument identifies gaps: no mention of encryption (data in transit or at rest could be intercepted), no mention of firewalls (network perimeter unprotected), no mention of a disaster recovery plan (if an incident does occur, recovery may be chaotic), and no mention of staff training (AUP alone does not guarantee staff understand current threats like phishing). Substantiated judgement — e.g. the hospital has strong physical and authentication controls but logical and policy gaps remain, particularly encryption and a formal recovery procedure, meaning the current measures are not fully sufficient.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two strengths and two weaknesses identified, with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points largely one-sided with limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a validation check?
A) A user types their password twice to confirm it matches
B) A staff member reads through a typed record against the original paper form
C) A system rejects a date of birth entered as 45/13/2010 because it is not a valid date format
D) A manager checks a printed report for errors before filing it
practice_questions.marks: C) A system rejects a date of birth entered as 45/13/2010 because it is not a valid date format [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two methods of automated data capture.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct automated methods from: barcode scanner / OCR (Optical Character Recognition) / OMR (Optical Mark Recognition) / magnetic stripe / chip reader / sensor / biometric scanner. Manual methods such as keyboard entry do not score. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between validation and verification in data entry.
practice_questions.marks: Validation (1 mark): an automated check by the computer that data is reasonable and in the correct format. Verification (1 mark): a check that data has been copied or transferred correctly from one place to another. Development / distinction (1 mark): a clear statement that validation cannot confirm data is factually true — it only checks plausibility — whereas verification confirms accuracy of transfer (e.g. double entry or proof reading). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A school uses an online form to enrol new students. Describe two different validation checks that could be applied to a field that asks for the student's age.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for each validation check described: one mark for naming the check type and one mark for applying it to the age field. For example: range check (1) — the age field only accepts values between 11 and 18, rejecting any number outside this range (1); type check (1) — the field only accepts numeric characters, rejecting letters or symbols (1). Other valid pairs: presence check (field cannot be left blank) + length check (age cannot exceed 3 digits). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A hospital is transferring patient records from paper files to a new digital database. Identify two possible sources of error during this process and, for each, suggest a technique that could be used to reduce that error.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each error source identified, one mark for each appropriate technique. For example: transcription error when typing (1) — use double entry / proof reading (1); transmission error if records are emailed to the database team (1) — use parity checking or checksum to verify data arrived intact (1). Other valid pairs: original source error (paper record was wrong) — verify against original medical notes before entry; deliberate falsification — restrict access to authorised data entry staff. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A supermarket uses barcodes and barcode scanners at every checkout. Explain how the check digit on a barcode helps to maintain data accuracy, and discuss what would happen if the check digit was not present.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clear explanation that the check digit is a mathematically calculated digit appended to the barcode; when a barcode is scanned the system recalculates the digit from the other numbers and compares it to the scanned value — a mismatch signals a scanning error. Discussion of consequences without check digit: a misread barcode digit would go undetected and the wrong product/price would be recorded; customers could be overcharged or undercharged; stock control data would be corrupted; the error would only be discovered much later when manual audits or customer complaints arise. Also effective at catching transposition errors.
Secure (3-4 marks): Check digit explained at a basic level with some consequence discussed.
Developing (2 marks): Describes that check digit detects errors but without sufficient explanation or consequences.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes an expert system?
A) A robot that assembles cars on a production line
B) Software that applies rules to a knowledge base to give advice as a human expert would
C) A database management system that stores patient records
D) A cloud platform that stores files remotely for any device to access
practice_questions.marks: B) Software that applies rules to a knowledge base to give advice as a human expert would [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which online banking improves efficiency for a business.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two: allows finance staff to make bulk payments quickly without visiting a bank branch; enables real-time cash flow monitoring; allows accounts to be reconciled automatically; payments can be authorised at any time rather than during banking hours; reduces paperwork associated with manual payment processing. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how payroll software improves efficiency for a large employer with 500 staff.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic point (e.g. it calculates wages automatically). 2 marks for development (e.g. payroll software calculates each employee's gross pay, deducts the correct tax and National Insurance, and transfers the net amount to their bank account, all without manual calculation). 3 marks for adding a further developed point or comparison (e.g. this reduces the risk of calculation errors that could lead to incorrect pay or legal penalties, and eliminates the need for a large accounts team to spend days processing pay manually each month). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A hospital uses an expert system to help doctors diagnose patients. Explain two ways this improves efficiency compared with relying entirely on a single doctor's knowledge.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per point identified, one mark per explanation. The expert system can access a far larger knowledge base than a single doctor can hold in memory, increasing the accuracy of diagnoses for rare conditions (2 marks). The system can process patient symptoms and return possible diagnoses almost instantly, whereas a doctor might need to consult textbooks or refer to a specialist, adding days to the patient's wait (2 marks). Accept any well-explained efficiency gain. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A logistics company is considering replacing its paper-based warehouse operation with robotic picking systems and wearable smart glasses for remaining staff.

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this change for the business.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Advantages — robotic picking operates 24/7 without fatigue, dramatically increasing throughput; robots are consistent, reducing picking errors; smart glasses overlay instructions, reducing training time and errors for new staff. Disadvantages — high upfront cost of robotic systems; risk of downtime if a robot fails (single point of failure); job losses may create negative publicity or legal challenges; staff will need retraining to work alongside robots. A balanced conclusion that acknowledges both the efficiency gains and the transition costs.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant points per side with some development.
Developing (2 marks): Mostly one-sided or undeveloped.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A further education college is reviewing its IT provision. Currently all lessons are delivered face-to-face, files are stored on local servers and student support materials are printed and distributed in class.

Evaluate the extent to which adopting online education, cloud computing and AI-based support tools would improve outcomes for students and reduce costs for the college.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Online education — students can revisit recorded lessons at their own pace, reducing the need for repeat teaching; blended learning allows more flexible timetabling; potentially reduces room usage costs. Cloud computing — eliminates local server maintenance costs; staff and students access files from any device or location; automatic off-site backup protects against data loss; scales without capital expenditure. AI support tools — intelligent tutoring systems provide immediate personalised feedback on assessments; AI chatbots answer common student queries out of hours. Counter-argument: reliable internet access is needed by all students (equity issue); staff require training; cyber security risks increase with cloud adoption; AI tools may give incorrect guidance if not carefully designed. Conclusion: the combination of all three is likely to reduce long-term costs and improve student flexibility, but the college must address the digital divide among students and invest in staff development and robust security measures before full adoption.
Secure (5–6 marks): Covers at least two of the three technologies with balanced argument and an attempt at a conclusion.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but limited balance or evaluation.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with little development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a Wide Area Network (WAN)?
A) A network that connects devices within a single school building
B) A network that connects devices across large geographical distances using external infrastructure
C) A private network accessible only to employees within one organisation
D) A network topology where all devices connect to a central hub
practice_questions.marks: B) A network that connects devices across large geographical distances using external infrastructure [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between a LAN and a WAN.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct differences: LAN covers a small/local area vs WAN covers a large/wide geographical area; LAN hardware is owned by the organisation vs WAN uses leased third-party infrastructure; LANs are typically faster and cheaper to run than WANs; LANs are more secure as they are physically confined to one site. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what a protocol is and why protocols are important in computer networks.
practice_questions.marks: Definition (1 mark): a protocol is a set of agreed rules and standards governing how data is formatted, transmitted and received across a network. Why important (2 marks): without protocols, devices from different manufacturers could not communicate (1 mark); protocols ensure all devices on a network follow the same rules so data is sent and received reliably, regardless of device or operating system (1 mark for a developed explanation). Named example adds quality but is not required for full marks. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A school is setting up a new computer network in its IT suite. Compare a star topology and a bus topology, identifying one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
practice_questions.marks: Star topology advantage (1 mark): if one device fails it does not affect the rest of the network / each device has a dedicated connection to the hub so performance is better. Star topology disadvantage (1 mark): if the central hub or switch fails the entire network goes down / requires more cable than a bus topology. Bus topology advantage (1 mark): cheaper to install as less cable is needed / easy to add devices to the backbone. Bus topology disadvantage (1 mark): if the backbone cable fails the entire network fails / performance degrades as more devices are added. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what packet sniffing is and describe one way an organisation can protect its data from this threat.
practice_questions.marks: Packet sniffing explanation (2 marks): software or hardware that intercepts and reads data packets as they travel across a network (1); on an unencrypted network the attacker can read sensitive information such as usernames, passwords and financial data in plain text (1). Protection method (2 marks): using encryption such as HTTPS / TLS (1) scrambles the data so that intercepted packets cannot be read without the decryption key (1). Other valid methods: VPN, using a secured/encrypted Wi-Fi network. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A rural village has no mobile phone signal and no cable broadband infrastructure. A local business needs reliable internet access to run its online shop.

Discuss which connectivity method or methods would be most suitable for this business, considering the advantages and disadvantages of each option.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Identifies satellite communication as the primary viable option given the absence of mobile and cable infrastructure. Advantages of satellite: works anywhere with a clear view of the sky, no reliance on ground infrastructure, can support broadband speeds with modern low-Earth orbit satellites. Disadvantages: higher latency with traditional geostationary satellites (which may affect real-time processes); equipment costs; monthly subscription. Considers whether 3G/4G/5G might be possible if partial signal exists with a booster. Microwave could work if the business has line-of-sight to a tower and the infrastructure is available. Wired Ethernet connects internal devices on site but cannot solve the last-mile connectivity problem. A substantiated recommendation is made (e.g. satellite is the only realistic option in this scenario, and low-Earth orbit satellite services are increasingly viable for rural businesses). Discusses trade-off between performance and cost.
Secure (5-6 marks): Satellite identified and discussed with advantages and disadvantages; at least one other method considered; recommendation attempted.
Developing (3-4 marks): One or two relevant methods identified but analysis is limited.
Emerging (1-2 marks): A basic relevant point with no development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a passive digital footprint?
A) Posting a comment on a social media platform
B) Uploading a photograph to an online gallery
C) A website logging your IP address without your direct input
D) Completing an online application form
practice_questions.marks: C) A website logging your IP address without your direct input [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two environmental problems caused by the disposal of digital devices (e-waste).
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: release of toxic/hazardous materials (lead, mercury, cadmium) into soil or water / illegal export to lower-income countries where it is unsafely processed / contamination of local ecosystems / harm to communities in processing areas. Answers that repeat the same idea score only 1 mark. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how teleworking can have both a positive and a negative effect on transport.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "teleworking reduces the number of commuters on the road"). Development of a positive effect scores 2 marks (e.g. "fewer daily commuter journeys means less road congestion and lower vehicle emissions, reducing the carbon footprint of those workers"). A negative counter-point scores 3 marks (e.g. "however, the growth of online shopping linked to home-based lifestyles has increased delivery vehicle journeys, which partially offsets the commuting reduction"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the digital divide and give one example of how it affects people at a local level.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): the digital divide is the gap between those who have reliable, affordable access to digital technology and the internet and those who do not; it can exist within a country (local) as well as between countries (global) (2 marks for a clear developed description covering both access and consequence; 1 mark for a basic definition without development).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, an elderly person in a rural area with no broadband connection cannot access online job boards, telehealth services or online banking, placing them at a significant disadvantage compared with well-connected urban residents (2 marks for a specific, applied example with the disadvantage identified; 1 mark for a vague example without identifying the impact). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the impact of social media on individuals and society, including both benefits and drawbacks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two benefits (e.g. global connection and community building; rapid sharing of important information; political participation; support networks for isolated individuals) and at least two drawbacks (e.g. cyberbullying linked to mental health problems; spread of fake news and misinformation; digital addiction and reduced attention span; privacy risks from oversharing personal data) with clear development and some reference to impact on real people or society.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two points on each side, briefly explained.
Developing (2 marks): Points largely one-sided or undeveloped.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A young person regularly posts personal updates, holiday photographs and location tags on a public social media profile. They have also signed up to several apps using the same email address and a simple password.

Evaluate the extent to which managing your digital footprint effectively can reduce the risk of identity theft and reputational harm.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying multiple active and passive footprint risks in the scenario (public posts reveal personal details; location tags enable tracking; reused simple passwords increase credential theft risk; passive data collected by apps). Explores how active management reduces risk (privacy settings limit public visibility; strong unique passwords and two-factor authentication reduce account compromise; careful review of what is posted protects reputation). Counter-argument acknowledges limits (passive data collection continues regardless of user choices; data brokers compile profiles from many sources; once data is shared it may be impossible to fully remove). A substantiated judgement — e.g. effective digital footprint management significantly reduces active risks but cannot eliminate passive data harvesting, so individuals should combine careful posting habits with regular privacy setting reviews and strong account security.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two points on each side of the argument, some applied to the scenario, with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with little development and no evaluative judgement. [8 marks]
